Using the engine in your own package

Source: vignettes/engine.qmd

This vignette is for the authors of other R packages. It shows how to copy the engine of inlavanilla into your package with use_vanilla(), how to keep the copy in step with the releases of inlavanilla, and how to call the engine from your own code. Users of inla_vanilla() do not need any of it.

The engine

The method of inlavanilla lives in the files R/vanilla-*.R, the engine. In this release there are 13 of them:

File Holds
vanilla-core.R vanilla_core(), which runs the stages of a fit
vanilla-laplace.R the posterior mode and the Laplace approximation
vanilla-vb.R the variational Bayes correction of the mean
vanilla-marginals.R the scans and the skew-normal marginals
vanilla-diagnostics.R the diagnostics of each stage, and the text of the warning
vanilla-sampling.R draws from the Gaussian copula of the marginals
vanilla-taylor.R LOO and WAIC by a Taylor expansion of the log-likelihood
vanilla-skew-normal.R the density, distribution and quantile functions of the skew-normal
vanilla-qsnorm-fast.R a fast approximation of skew-normal quantiles (Apache License 2.0, Thomas Luu)
vanilla-control.R vanilla_control() and the checks of control
vanilla-parallel.R the optional parallel scans
vanilla-progress.R the progress lines
vanilla-utils.R finite differences, errors and warnings, and the checks of arguments

The method is that of INLAvaan (Jamil & Rue, 2026a, 2026b), with no latent field and nothing specific to a model. Everything that users of inlavanilla see, such as inla_vanilla(), its methods and its help pages, is in the other files of R/. The engine is internal code only: it exports nothing, has no roxygen and no S3 methods, and does not name the package it is in.

Why copy the engine, and not import it? inlavanilla is not on CRAN, and the engine is not exported, so a package on CRAN cannot import it. A copy makes your package self-contained: it runs without inlavanilla, and takes a new release of the engine only when you choose. INLAvaan holds engine files in this way.

Copying the engine

Run use_vanilla() from the root of your package:

inlavanilla::use_vanilla(release = "v26.11.24")
── Copying the engine of inlavanilla into mypkg ──

✔ Wrote the lock 'inst/inlavanilla.lock'.
✔ Added the engine's copyright holders to Authors@R in 'DESCRIPTION', with
  the role "cph": Haziq Jamil and Thomas Luu.
✔ Added cli (>= 3.6.0), stats and utils to Imports in 'DESCRIPTION'.
✔ Added future and parallelly to Suggests in 'DESCRIPTION'.
✔ Raised R in Depends to `(>= 4.1.0)`, from `(>= 3.5)`.
✔ No engine object has the name of another object in 'R/' or of an import
  in 'NAMESPACE'.
ℹ v26.11.24-1, a newer release, exists:
  `inlavanilla::use_vanilla("v26.11.24-1")` updates to it.

── Still to do ──

☐ Write the function that calls `vanilla_core()` with your model's
  log-posterior and turns the list it returns into your results.
  `vignette("engine", package = "inlavanilla")` shows how, and so does
  <https://haziqj.ml/inlavanilla/articles/engine.html>.
☐ Run `devtools::document()`.

☐ Add a NEWS bullet that names the release, such as "Uses the engine of
  inlavanilla v26.11.24."

── Optional ──

• `inlavanilla::use_vanilla_test()` writes a test that fails when an engine
  file differs from the lock.
• `inlavanilla::use_vanilla_ci()` adds a GitHub Actions workflow that runs
  `vanilla_status()` on every push.

use_vanilla() copies the engine files of a release byte for byte into R/, and lists them in the lock inst/inlavanilla.lock. It also adds to DESCRIPTION what the engine needs, where it is missing: the copyright holders of the engine in Authors@R, with the role "cph"; cli (>= 3.6.0), stats and utils in Imports; future and parallelly in Suggests; and R (>= 4.1.0) in Depends. It edits only the lines of those fields, and never removes anything. A copyright holder who is already in Authors@R is not added again, and an entry without the role "cph" is left as it is, with an item in the list of what is still to do.

By default the release is that of the inlavanilla installed on your computer, or, when that version is not a release, the newest release before it. Give release to copy another one. The files come from the release on GitHub, which needs the internet but not git. To copy without the internet, give clone, the path of a local clone of inlavanilla, which needs git.

Some rules keep the copy safe to update:

  • Never edit an engine file. The next update would undo the edit, so use_vanilla() stops, and changes nothing, when a copy differs from the lock. Report a problem with the engine at https://github.com/haziqj/inlavanilla/issues instead.
  • The names R/vanilla-*.R are kept for the engine. Give your own files other names.
  • Leave the engine files out of your code formatter and linter, such as air, styler or lintr, so that they stay byte for byte.
  • Do not list inlavanilla in your DESCRIPTION: your package does not need it.

The lock

The lock records where the copy came from:

Upstream: https://github.com/haziqj/inlavanilla
Release: v26.11.24
Commit: 88056cfa545cee5a601af4485bbc2a3a5443e0fc
Version: 26.11.24
Synced: 2026-11-25
Hash: md5 of the text with LF line endings

File: R/vanilla-control.R
MD5: 58d754b181b188bfda7d5f09d88bd0c3

File: R/vanilla-core.R
MD5: aa682883cae63b63b2f41b94c94f019d

and so on for each engine file.

Field Holds
Upstream the repository of inlavanilla
Release the release copied, a tag on GitHub
Commit the commit of that tag
Version the version of inlavanilla at that commit
Synced the day of the copy
Hash how the hashes are taken
File, MD5 each engine file, and its hash

The hash is the MD5 of the text with its carriage returns removed, so that a checkout with Windows line endings matches. The lock is installed with your package, so you can read it at run time, for example to say which release of the engine a fit used:

read.dcf(system.file("inlavanilla.lock", package = "mypkg"))[1, "Release"]

Checking the copy

vanilla_status() checks the copy, with one line per check:

inlavanilla::vanilla_status()
── Engine copy in mypkg ──

ℹ inlavanilla v26.11.24, commit 88056cf: 13 files, copied on 2026-11-25.
✔ The lock 'inst/inlavanilla.lock' is well formed.
✔ The 13 engine files match the lock.
✔ No engine object has the name of another object in 'R/' or of an import
  in 'NAMESPACE'.
✔ 'DESCRIPTION' has the engine's dependencies and `R (>= 4.1.0)`.
✔ Authors@R names the engine's copyright holders: Haziq Jamil and Thomas
  Luu.
✔ The license, "GPL (>= 3)", allows the engine's license, "GPL (>= 3)".
✔ The lock matches release v26.11.24 on GitHub.
! A newer release changes copied files: v26.11.24-1 changes
  'R/vanilla-qsnorm-fast.R' and 'R/vanilla-skew-normal.R'.
  Changes:
  <https://github.com/haziqj/inlavanilla/compare/v26.11.24...v26.11.24-1>
→ Update with `inlavanilla::use_vanilla(release = "v26.11.24-1")`, then run
  your tests.

The checks:

  • Lock: the lock exists and can be read.
  • Copies: each engine file has the hash in the lock, and every file R/vanilla-*.R is in the lock.
  • Names: no object of the engine has the name of another object in R/, or of a name that NAMESPACE imports. R keeps one of the two with no warning, so a clash breaks the engine or your own code silently.
  • Dependencies and authors: DESCRIPTION has what use_vanilla() adds.
  • License: your license allows code under GPL version 3 or later (see “Licensing” below).
  • Release: the lock matches its release on GitHub.
  • Update: whether a newer release changes a copied file. A newer release is reported, and is not a failure.

The last two checks need GitHub, or a clone given as clone. Without either, they are skipped with a note, and the others still run. In continuous integration, vanilla_status(error = TRUE) stops with an error when a check fails. A skipped check, or a line marked with !, is never an error.

Two optional helpers put these checks where they run by themselves. use_vanilla_test() writes the test file tests/testthat/test-vanilla-engine.R, which fails when an engine file differs from the lock. It uses base R and testthat only, so your package does not need inlavanilla to run it. It reads the source files in R/, so it runs under devtools::test() and skips under R CMD check. use_vanilla_ci() writes the GitHub Actions workflow .github/workflows/vanilla-status.yaml, which runs the checks on every push:

      - name: Install inlavanilla
        shell: Rscript {0}
        run: |
          install.packages("remotes")
          remotes::install_github("haziqj/inlavanilla@*release")

      - name: Check the engine copy
        shell: Rscript {0}
        run: inlavanilla::vanilla_status(error = TRUE)

Updating

When vanilla_status() reports a newer release, update the copy with use_vanilla() and that release:

inlavanilla::use_vanilla(release = "v26.11.24-1")
── Updating the engine of inlavanilla in mypkg ──

✔ Copied 13 engine files to 'R/': 2 changed, 11 unchanged.
  Changed: 'R/vanilla-qsnorm-fast.R' and 'R/vanilla-skew-normal.R'.
✔ Updated the lock 'inst/inlavanilla.lock'.
✔ 'DESCRIPTION' already has what the engine needs.
✔ No engine object has the name of another object in 'R/' or of an import
  in 'NAMESPACE'.

Read the NEWS of the release and the changes to the engine, run your tests and R CMD check, add a NEWS bullet that names the release, and commit the engine files, the lock and DESCRIPTION together.

The interface of the engine is the 25 objects that the next section documents: vanilla_core(), vanilla_control(), check_control(), diagnostics_internal(), diagnostic_problems(), advice_entries, check_flags(), param_flags(), warn_levels, summary_levels, sn_draws(), dsnorm(), psnorm(), qsnorm(), sn_moments(), sn_mode(), sn_score_map(), taylor_terms(), taylor_loo(), taylor_waic(), taylor_trace(), cov_root(), abort(), warn() and warning_text(), the names in interface below. They change only with a NEWS bullet of inlavanilla that says so. Everything else in the engine may change in any release.

The interface

After use_vanilla(), the functions of the engine are internal functions of your package, and your code calls them by name. In this vignette we take inlavanilla’s own:

# After use_vanilla() these are internal functions of your package. Here we
# take inlavanilla's own.
interface <- c(
  "vanilla_core", "vanilla_control", "check_control",
  "diagnostics_internal", "diagnostic_problems", "advice_entries",
  "check_flags", "param_flags", "warn_levels", "summary_levels",
  "sn_draws", "dsnorm", "psnorm", "qsnorm", "sn_moments", "sn_mode",
  "sn_score_map", "taylor_terms", "taylor_loo", "taylor_waic",
  "taylor_trace", "cov_root", "abort", "warn", "warning_text"
)
for (f in interface) {
  assign(f, utils::getFromNamespace(f, "inlavanilla"))
}

vanilla_core() 

vanilla_core(
  lp, gr = NULL, init, hess = NULL, hess_mode = NULL,
  gaussian_marginals = NULL,
  vb_correction = c("onestep", "full", "none"),
  marginals = c("skewnorm", "gaussian"),
  marginal_scan = c("linear", "exact", "laplace", "plain"),
  tk_fallback = FALSE, cores = NULL, control = list(),
  verbose = FALSE, silent = FALSE
)
Argument Meaning
lp the log-posterior, a function of the parameter vector alone
gr its gradient, or NULL
init the starting values, a named numeric vector
hess its Hessian, or NULL; needs gr
hess_mode a Hessian called at the mode only (see “The two hooks”)
gaussian_marginals parameters whose marginal is taken as Gaussian (see “The two hooks”)
vb_correction, marginals, marginal_scan, tk_fallback, cores, control, verbose, silent as in inla_vanilla()

What the core expects of your functions:

  • theta arrives as a numeric vector named as init, in its order. Names mean nothing to the core: a prefix such as log_ is only a name, and any transform is yours.
  • lp returns the log of the joint density of the data and the parameters, with any Jacobian. Keep the normalising constants, since they enter the log marginal likelihood logml. Return -Inf where the model cannot be evaluated. NA, NaN and any value at or below -1e39 count as failures too.
  • gr is the gradient of lp, not of minus lp. Where lp fails, gr must not return a finite value: the VB correction and the ridge bend call gr alone at some points.
  • hess may return a matrix, a sparse Matrix, or a number when there is one parameter.
  • There are no dots: bind the data in closures, as below.

Fit a Poisson regression to eight points:

x <- c(-1.75, -1.25, -0.75, -0.25, 0.25, 0.75, 1.25, 1.75)
y <- c(1, 0, 2, 1, 3, 4, 2, 6)
lp <- function(theta) {
  eta <- theta[["b0"]] + theta[["b1"]] * x
  sum(stats::dpois(y, exp(eta), log = TRUE)) +
    sum(stats::dnorm(theta, 0, 10, log = TRUE))
}
gr <- function(theta) {
  r <- y - exp(theta[["b0"]] + theta[["b1"]] * x)
  c(sum(r), sum(r * x)) - theta / 100
}
core <- vanilla_core(lp, gr, init = c(b0 = 0, b1 = 0))
#> ✔ Found the posterior mode in 8 iterations [11ms]
#> ✔ VB mean correction, max shift 0.25σ [15ms]
#> ✔ Fitted 2 skew-normal marginals [9ms]

What it returns

vanilla_core() returns a plain list:

str(core, max.level = 1, give.attr = FALSE)
#> List of 21
#>  $ mode         : Named num [1:2] 0.655 0.578
#>  $ mean_vb      : Named num [1:2] 0.586 0.6
#>  $ cov          : num [1:2, 1:2] 0.0777 -0.0359 -0.0359 0.0516
#>  $ sn           : num [1:2, 1:9] 0.853 0.435 0.394 0.276 -1.615 ...
#>  $ logml        : num -19.4
#>  $ logml_laplace: num -19.4
#>  $ lp_max       : num -18.3
#>  $ opt          :List of 6
#>  $ restart      : NULL
#>  $ diagnostics  :List of 3
#>  $ scan         :List of 4
#>  $ timing       : Named num [1:6] 0.001 0.013 0.016 0.009 0.001 ...
#>  $ counts       : Named int [1:3] 75 32 0
#>  $ vb_correction: chr "onestep"
#>  $ marginals    : chr "skewnorm"
#>  $ marginal_scan: chr "linear"
#>  $ tk_fallback  : logi FALSE
#>  $ fallback     : chr(0) 
#>  $ cores        : NULL
#>  $ workers      : int 1
#>  $ has_grad     : logi TRUE
Field Holds
mode the posterior mode
mean_vb the mean after the VB correction (the mode without it)
cov the covariance of the Laplace approximation
sn the marginals, a row per parameter (below)
logml, logml_laplace the log marginal likelihood, and its Laplace part
lp_max the log-posterior at the mode
opt, restart the result of nlminb(), and of its restart, if any
diagnostics the diagnostics of each stage: optim, vb and marginals
scan the scans of the marginals, NULL for Gaussian marginals
timing, counts the time of each stage, and the calls of lp, gr and hess
vb_correction, marginals, marginal_scan, tk_fallback the settings used
fallback the parameters rescanned by tk_fallback
cores, workers the setting of cores, and the workers used
has_grad whether gr was given

The columns of sn are the location xi, scale omega and shape alpha of each skew-normal, and the scan diagnostics gamma1, nmad, tails, ridge_bend, logC and unscanned_mass, which vignette("diagnostics", package = "inlavanilla") explains:

round(core$sn, 3)
#>       xi omega  alpha gamma1  nmad tails ridge_bend  logC unscanned_mass
#> b0 0.853 0.394 -1.615 -0.069 0.010     1      0.040 0.941          0.001
#> b1 0.435 0.276  1.084  0.000 0.015     1      0.146 0.909          0.000

What it prints and signals

The core prints a line as each stage ends, as messages. silent = TRUE prints nothing, and verbose = TRUE adds the details of each stage. Its errors and warnings have the classes inlavanilla_error and inlavanilla_warning, and warning_text(w) gives the text of a warning without colours or line breaks. The engine raises them with abort(message, class = NULL, parent = NULL, call = NULL, .envir = parent.frame()) and warn(message, class = NULL, .envir = parent.frame()), which you can use for your own conditions too: message is a cli template, wrapped to the width of the output, class adds your classes before the engine’s, and parent, an error that caused this one, has its message appended. The core installs no condition handler: catch what you need, as here, where the warnings of a fit are recorded and not shown:

seen <- character()
core2 <- withCallingHandlers(
  vanilla_core(lp, gr, init = c(b0 = 0, b1 = 0), silent = TRUE),
  warning = function(w) {
    seen <<- unique(c(seen, warning_text(w)))
    tryInvokeRestart("muffleWarning")
  }
)
seen
#> character(0)

Some messages of the engine still name inlavanilla’s interface: they call the log-posterior logpost and the gradient grad, two errors are reported as coming from inla_vanilla(), and the note on parallel workers points to ?inla_vanilla. A later release will word them for any package.

The parallel scans load your package on each worker, by the name that utils::packageName() gives, so the package must be installed: under devtools::load_all(), use cores = 1.

vanilla_control() builds the list for the argument control, with the defaults of inlavanilla. check_control(control) checks a plain list, from vanilla_control() or written by hand: an entry without a name, or with a name that vanilla_control() does not have, is an error, and the result is the list completed with the defaults. vanilla_core() calls it on its control, so call it yourself only to check a control before the fit starts. To offer vanilla_control() to your users, document and export it from a file of your own, as inlavanilla’s R/control.R does.

The two hooks

Two arguments of vanilla_core() are not in inla_vanilla(), for packages that know more about their models:

  • hess_mode, a function that gives the Hessian at the mode only. It is called once, or twice after a restart of the mode search, and never by nlminb(), the VB correction or the scans. It needs gr, and is checked against the differences of gr and for symmetry.
  • gaussian_marginals, the names or indices of parameters whose marginal may be taken as Gaussian: the log-posterior is quadratic along each of their axes, and those axes are nearly separate from the other parameters, as with saturated intercepts, but not random effects. They get no scan, their VB shift is held at zero, and their marginal is N(mode, \(\Sigma_{jj}\)), with NA in the scan columns.
set.seed(2)
z <- stats::rnorm(40, 3, 1.5)
lp_normal <- function(theta) {
  sigma <- exp(theta[["log_sigma"]])
  sum(stats::dnorm(z, theta[["mu"]], sigma, log = TRUE)) +
    stats::dnorm(theta[["mu"]], 0, 10, log = TRUE) +
    stats::dexp(sigma, log = TRUE) +
    theta[["log_sigma"]]
}
core_normal <- vanilla_core(
  lp_normal,
  init = c(mu = 0, log_sigma = 0),
  gaussian_marginals = "mu",
  silent = TRUE
)
round(core_normal$sn, 3)
#>              xi omega alpha gamma1  nmad tails ridge_bend logC
#> mu        3.144 0.258 0.000     NA    NA    NA         NA   NA
#> log_sigma 0.426 0.143 1.237   0.11 0.007     1          0 0.94
#>           unscanned_mass
#> mu                    NA
#> log_sigma              0

Diagnostics and the warning

diagnostics_internal() turns the diagnostics of the stages into a global and a per-parameter table, check_flags() and param_flags() say which checks are off, at the levels in warn_levels and summary_levels:

dg <- diagnostics_internal(
  core$diagnostics$optim,
  core$diagnostics$vb,
  core$diagnostics$marginals,
  pars = core$mean_vb
)
check_flags(dg, gaussian = FALSE)
#>       grad_gap           mode        vb_step        vb_gain      hess_cond 
#>          FALSE          FALSE          FALSE          FALSE          FALSE 
#>             vb           nmad unscanned_mass          tails     ridge_bend 
#>          FALSE          FALSE          FALSE          FALSE          FALSE 
#>       mean_gap 
#>          FALSE

diagnostic_problems(dg, gaussian, has_grad, advice) gives the bullets of a warning, one per flagged check, worded by you. advice is a list with the entries of advice_entries, cli templates that name your own arguments:

advice_entries
#> [1] "grad_gap"   "no_grad"    "vb_full"    "vb_none"    "mode_limit"
#> [6] "mode_retry" "funnel"
poisson_advice <- list(
  grad_gap = "the gradient of the Poisson model does not match its
    log-posterior",
  no_grad = "",
  vb_full = "{.code fit_poisson(vb_correction = \"full\")}",
  vb_none = "{.code fit_poisson(vb_correction = \"none\")}",
  mode_limit = "Raise {.code mode_maxit} in {.arg control}.",
  mode_retry = "Check the data: a rate of zero has no finite log.",
  funnel = "Check that the data are counts."
)
diagnostic_problems(dg, FALSE, core$has_grad, poisson_advice)
#> character(0)
#> attr(,"envir")
#> <environment: 0x62e1d90da4f8>

A healthy fit has no problems. When there are some, raise them with warn(c(header, problems), class = ..., .envir = attr(problems, "envir")), as the example below does. inlavanilla’s own wording is inlavanilla_advice in its file R/diagnostics.R.

Draws and the skew-normal functions

sn_draws(sn, cov, nsamp, corr = stats::cov2cor(cov)) draws from the Gaussian copula of the marginals:

set.seed(1)
draws <- sn_draws(core$sn, core$cov, nsamp = 4000)
round(colMeans(draws), 3)
#>    b0    b1 
#> 0.585 0.595
Function Gives
dsnorm(x, xi, omega, alpha, logC = 0, log = FALSE) the density
psnorm(q, xi = 0, omega = 1, alpha = 0, lower_tail = TRUE) the distribution function
qsnorm(p, xi = 0, omega = 1, alpha = 0) the quantile function
sn_moments(xi, omega, alpha) the mean and SD, as a list
sn_mode(xi, omega, alpha) the mode
sn_score_map(xi, omega, alpha, zmax = 7, n_knots = 141L) a function from normal scores to quantiles, for draws: a spline through n_knots knots from -zmax to zmax, linear beyond

LOO and WAIC

taylor_terms() gives the terms of LOO and WAIC by a second-order Taylor expansion of each unit’s log-likelihood around the posterior (Alhyari et al., 2026). Your code supplies, at mean_vb and for each unit, the log-likelihood, the score and the Hessian, by whatever route it has: taylor_terms(l, s, H = NULL, Omega, root = cov_root(Omega)), where s is the matrix of scores with a row per unit, H the array of Hessians, and root any matrix \(A\) with \(A A^\top = \Omega\), by default cov_root(Omega), which gives the same terms whichever root is taken. With derivatives already in whitened coordinates, give Omega = root = diag(m).

Then taylor_loo(terms) and taylor_waic(terms) give the estimates. Where a unit has no second-order term (for the LOO, a leverage of 1 or more), each falls back to the first order for every unit by itself: its order is then 1, and first_order lists the units that sent it there.

taylor_trace(terms, what), with what either "loo" or "waic", is a cheaper estimate for when only the diagonal of each unit’s Hessian is known. It uses the scores and each unit’s total leverage \(k_u = -\operatorname{tr}(\Omega H_u)\) alone, so call taylor_terms() with H = NULL and then set terms$k_sum to \(k_u\): with the derivatives in whitened coordinates, terms$k_sum <- -rowSums(D), where D holds the diagonal of each unit’s Hessian, a row per unit. Its over lists the units whose leverages add up to 1 or more, for which the estimate may be poor. inlavanilla’s loo() takes this route for hessian = "diagonal".

theta <- core$mean_vb
mu <- exp(theta[["b0"]] + theta[["b1"]] * x)
X <- cbind(1, x)
l <- stats::dpois(y, mu, log = TRUE)
s <- (y - mu) * X
H <- array(0, c(2, 2, length(y)))
for (u in seq_along(y)) {
  H[, , u] <- -mu[u] * tcrossprod(X[u, ])
}
terms <- taylor_terms(l, s, H, Omega = core$cov)
taylor_loo(terms)$estimates
#>           Estimate        SE
#> elpd_loo -13.56621 1.3465305
#> p_loo      1.20383 0.2902777
#> looic     27.13242 2.6930610
taylor_waic(terms)$estimates
#>             Estimate        SE
#> elpd_waic -13.457814 1.3039788
#> p_waic      1.095435 0.2404797
#> waic       26.915629 2.6079575

A small example

fit_poisson() is a complete adapter: it builds the log-posterior from the data, calls vanilla_core(), raises its own warning, and turns the result into a summary.

# grad_scale scales the gradient of b1, only to show a wrong gradient below
fit_poisson <- function(y, x, vb_correction = "onestep", silent = FALSE,
                        grad_scale = 1) {
  logpost <- function(theta) {
    eta <- theta[["b0"]] + theta[["b1"]] * x
    sum(stats::dpois(y, exp(eta), log = TRUE)) +
      sum(stats::dnorm(theta, 0, 10, log = TRUE))
  }
  grad <- function(theta) {
    r <- y - exp(theta[["b0"]] + theta[["b1"]] * x)
    c(sum(r), grad_scale * sum(r * x)) - theta / 100
  }
  core <- vanilla_core(
    logpost,
    grad,
    init = c(b0 = 0, b1 = 0),
    vb_correction = vb_correction,
    silent = silent
  )
  dg <- diagnostics_internal(
    core$diagnostics$optim,
    core$diagnostics$vb,
    core$diagnostics$marginals,
    pars = core$mean_vb
  )
  problems <- diagnostic_problems(
    dg,
    gaussian = core$marginals == "gaussian",
    has_grad = core$has_grad,
    advice = poisson_advice
  )
  if (length(problems) > 0) {
    warn(
      c("The Poisson fit may be inaccurate:", problems),
      class = "mypkg_diagnostics_warning",
      .envir = attr(problems, "envir")
    )
  }
  sn <- core$sn
  mom <- sn_moments(sn[, "xi"], sn[, "omega"], sn[, "alpha"])
  summary <- data.frame(
    mean = mom$mean,
    sd = mom$sd,
    lower = qsnorm(0.025, sn[, "xi"], sn[, "omega"], sn[, "alpha"]),
    upper = qsnorm(0.975, sn[, "xi"], sn[, "omega"], sn[, "alpha"]),
    row.names = rownames(sn)
  )
  structure(list(summary = summary, core = core), class = "poisson_fit")
}

print.poisson_fit <- function(x, ...) {
  print(x$summary, digits = 3)
  invisible(x)
}
fit_poisson(y, x, silent = TRUE)
#>     mean    sd   lower upper
#> b0 0.586 0.289 -0.0292  1.11
#> b1 0.597 0.224  0.1752  1.05

Here, on purpose, the gradient of b1 is 30% too large. The fit still runs, and the adapter’s warning names the problem in its own words:

fit_poisson(y, x, silent = TRUE, grad_scale = 1.3)
#> Warning: `grad` does not look like the gradient of `logpost`.
#> ✖ Its Jacobian at the mode is not symmetric (relative asymmetry 0.15), as
#>   the Hessian of a function must be.
#> ℹ A wrong gradient gives a wrong mode and wrong marginals.
#> Warning: The Poisson fit may be inaccurate:
#> ✖ the gradient of the Poisson model does not match its log-posterior at the
#>   mode (gap > 0.1) for `b1` (0.15).
#> ℹ A wrong gradient gives a wrong log marginal likelihood, and can move the
#>   mode and the covariance.
#>     mean    sd    lower upper
#> b0 0.597 0.286 -0.00869  1.12
#> b1 0.602 0.224  0.18616  1.07

The first warning comes from the engine, and names inlavanilla’s grad and logpost, as said above. The second is the adapter’s own.

inlavanilla’s inla_vanilla(), in its file R/inla-vanilla.R, is the full reference adapter: it checks the arguments, sets up the condition handlers, reads the transforms from the names of the parameters, and builds the fit.

Licensing

The engine is under the GNU General Public License, version 3 or later, so a package that holds it must be distributed under GPL-3 or GPL (>= 3) too (see the GNU GPL FAQ). Keep the headers of the engine files. vanilla-qsnorm-fast.R is Thomas Luu’s code under the Apache License 2.0, which GPL version 3 allows. The "cph" entries that use_vanilla() adds to Authors@R name the copyright holders of the engine, so that the ownership of all the code of your package is clear, as CRAN’s policy asks.

use_vanilla() and vanilla_status() warn when the License of your package does not allow the engine’s. If your package cannot be under the GPL, ask at https://github.com/haziqj/inlavanilla/issues.
